title: Newborn glomerular function and gestational particulate air pollution.
ehr_evidence: The data source was the ENVIRONAGE birth cohort (mother–newborn pairs recruited at delivery at the East-Limburg Hospital, Genk, Belgium), with data from questionnaires, cord blood biospecimens, and modeled ambient air pollution exposure — not electronic health records.
summary: In this prospective birth cohort of 1484 healthy term newborns and their mothers in Belgium, higher gestational exposure to particulate air pollution (black carbon and PM2.5) was associated with elevated cord blood cystatin C, a marker of glomerular function.
key_findings: Each 0.5 μg/m3 increment in gestational black carbon (BC) exposure was associated with a 0.04 mg/L (95% CI 0.01–0.07; p<0.01) increase in cord blood cystatin C.
Each 5 μg/m3 increment in PM2.5 exposure was associated with a 0.07 mg/L (95% CI 0.03–0.11; p<0.01) increase in cord blood cystatin C.

Third-trimester exposure showed similar significant associations (PM2.5 0.06 mg/L, 95% CI 0.04–0.09; BC 0.04 mg/L, 95% CI 0.00–0.08; p<0.02), while no significant associations were observed for first and second trimester.
A 0.5 μg/m3 increase in BC exposure was associated with a 37% higher risk (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.04, 1.80) of having cord blood cystatin C above the 10th percentile.
A 5 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 exposure was associated with an 80% higher risk (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.23, 2.65) of having cord blood cystatin C above the 10th percentile.

Distributed lag models identified the beginning of the third trimester (week 27 onwards) as the most significant exposure window for both BC and PM2.5 in association with elevated cord blood cystatin C.
pathologies_diseases: glomerular kidney function (cord blood cystatin C as marker of glomerular filtration rate)
data_source_type: biospecimen (cord blood) within a birth cohort
population: 1484 healthy term newborns and their mothers from the ENVIRONAGE birth cohort recruited at East-Limburg Hospital, Genk, Belgium (2010–2020)
exposure_domain: air pollution (particulate matter PM2.5 and black carbon)
limitations: No other kidney function markers (e.g., creatinine) reflecting tubular function were available.
Exposure was estimated from modeled residential air pollution rather than individual monitoring.
Observational design with potential residual confounding.
Single cord blood measurement at birth limits inference about sustained kidney function.
